summary: Liraasa 2.5, step 2: the author's decisions on the 2.3 grammar audit (review/grammar_spec_2_3.md), rulings 2.5:G88-G128 in the patch's order. Amended rulings are marked amended_by, superseded ones superseded_by; a ruling example that no longer holds is archived. rulings.topic: Questions end in ki; a fronted ki-word may drop it
rulings.ruling: A yes/no question ends in ki. A content question ends in ki unless its ki-word is the first word of the sentence; a ki-word left in its answer's place requires the final ki. This exception covers ki-coda, ki-pago, ki-krono, ki-nela, ki-nela de, ki-kasa, manner ki-modo and ki-muya-krono only. Questions with ki-eli + noun, ki-muya + noun and degree ki-modo + adjective always end in ki (2.3:G76, 2.2:G61 stand), and the same three without ki remain exclamations. Embedded questions never take ki (2.3:G77 stands). A ki-word in its answer's place in a clause without final ki is an embedded question or part of a statement, never a direct question.
examples: Ki-kasa taivo po amora maivo ki?
Maivo po masuma li talirivo ki-kasa.
examples_ungrammatical: ki-word in place without final ki is not a question
ki-eli + noun questions always end in ki
rulings.notes: This also resolves I-02 (three live statements of the question rule).

rulings.topic: Which clause a final ki or attitude word belongs to
rulings.ruling: A ki or attitude word (seye, mufe, poye, pifu, zoke) at the end of a sentence belongs to the main clause, even when a subordinate clause follows it. Doubt inside a trailing subordinate clause is expressed with a modal (nosi); an embedded yes/no question uses ki-oro. ki is the last word of the sentence, except that a vocative set off by a comma may follow it.
examples: Taivo sabesia fime maivo lirala poye.
Perhaps you know that I sing.
Taivo sabesia fime maivo nosi lirala.
You know that I might sing.
Taivo sabesia fime maivo lirala ki?
Do you know that I sing?
rulings.notes: 0.8:G4 (ki may also close the main clause before an appended direct quotation) stands.

rulings.topic: The clause's closing order and its edge positions
rulings.ruling: A clause closes in this order: … VERB [OBJECT] [ADJUNCTS] [fuyi] [STATUS: hoyo | yasmo] [ATTITUDE] [ki]. Closing time words, durations and clause-final reve / loki stand among the adjuncts, before fuyi. Outside the core slots, a clause has edge positions. Before it, in order: a line linker (ata, oro, nara), FRAME, TOPIC, then a fronted ki-word (2.5:G88). After it: a vocative set off by a comma, which may follow ki.
examples: May we always sing to each other.
Taivo viki pagopa ligo maivo ki, maivo de amor?
Would you come near me, my love?
amends: 2.3:G78 (closing order only; its other clauses stand)
derived: The edge positions (line linker, FRAME, TOPIC, fronted ki-word; vocative after the clause) were part of the lean, not option A itself. They are needed to make 2.5:G88 and the existing line-initial ata / vocative rulings fit the template. Confirm.
Durations and clause-final reve / loki sit among the adjuncts, like closing time words. Confirm.
rulings.notes: This also resolves I-03 (constructions the rulings allow but the template had no slot for).

rulings.ruling: FRAME, the clause-opening slot set off by a comma, holds a time adverbial or a place adverbial. Tense words (po, futu, pressa) and iteration words (reve, loki, bodu) are not frame words and are never closing time words.
examples_ungrammatical: po is a tense word, not a closing time word
derived: 'Place adverbial' covers place correlatives (eli-pago, ola-pago, toda-pago …) and prepositional phrases of place (En li nimu, …). Confirm.

rulings.ruling: A command is marked. In writing it ends in '!' or contains fisa; in speech, fisa or command intonation marks it. A subjectless, tenseless clause with neither mark is an elliptical statement, not a command.
derived: In speech, command intonation stands in for the written '!'. Confirm.
rulings.notes: I-42 (which operators a command may carry; yava's position with a FRAME) was not decided. See author_inputs_needed.

rulings.ruling: A fragment question follows the ki rule: it ends in ki.
Echo ki attaches only to a single word or a bare noun phrase. raho + clause + ki is therefore always a direct question (2.3:G74 stands).

rulings.topic: ke and ka: one contrast for every predicate
rulings.ruling: ke and ka mark one contrast for every kind of predicate (adjective, noun phrase or location): ke = holds now, or for a time; ka = lasting, defining, by nature.
supersedes: clause.copulas definitions of ke and ka
examples: Li kavbikova ke su li tabu.
The basket is on the table (right now).
Li nimu ka ligo li cilni.
The home is near the city (it always has been).
I was a little child (back then).
I am a singer (it's who I am).
The person is good at the moment.
The friend is good by nature.

rulings.ruling: The minimal clause is SUBJECT + VERB, with these exceptions: commands, hortatives, permitted ellipsis, existential miyo clauses (which have no subject), and bare adjective predicates. A bare adjective predicate (SUBJECT ADJECTIVE, no copula) is allowed only in the present with no operators; anything more needs ke or ka.
examples: Miyo baba sora en li nimu.
There is a friend in the home.
examples_ungrammatical: a bare adjective predicate takes no operators
a bare adjective predicate takes no operators
rulings.notes: A bare predicate carries no ke / ka contrast (2.5:G93); use a copula when that contrast matters.

rulings.ruling: po ka = was (lasting), with no claim about now. kapoki = was, and no longer is. (With 2.5:G93, po ke = was, at that time.)
examples: They were good (no claim about now).
They were good, and no longer are.

rulings.topic: Kinship nouns are not names for possession
rulings.ruling: Kinship nouns (pilo, mare and the rest) are never treated as names for possession. Only a pronoun, or a personal name standing before de, is the owner; otherwise X de Y = 'X of Y' (Y owns). When both sides are personal names, the left one owns.
derived: Two names: the left one owns. The author chose C; this follows from 1.2:G27 (a name before de owns) and is listed for confirmation.

rulings.ruling: Chains of de group from the left: X de Y de Z = (X de Y) de Z. The ownership rules apply first to X de Y, then to that whole phrase de Z.
examples: li suma de maivo de yuge
my warmth, of the body  [(li suma de maivo) de yuge]
rulings.translator_preference: When the intended meaning groups from the right ('the warmth of my body'), do not produce a three-part chain. Rephrase, for example with an adjective form or a second sentence.

rulings.ruling: NUMBER de NUMBER may be a fraction or a partitive; context decides. Fractions are written with spaces (tressa de cuara), never hyphenated.
examples: One of the two will return / One half will return.
rulings.translator_preference: For a partitive, prefer an article (una de li dossa) so the output is not ambiguous.

rulings.ruling: Noun-phrase order: [QUANTIFIER] [DETERMINER: li | baba | eli | ola | eliri | olari | ki-eli | OWNER de] [ORDINAL] [NUMBER] {[DEGREE WORD] ADJECTIVE} NOUN[-ti][-ri] [de NP] [raho CLAUSE]. The ordinal stands right after the determiner, before the adjectives. Degree words (ruli, kasi, menu, mosa, lusu, gase, diba) stand directly before the adjective they modify. ki-muya fills the QUANTIFIER slot. OWNER de takes only a pronoun or a personal name (2.5:G95).
derived: ORDINAL before NUMBER (li una-ne dossa lirari, 'the first two songs'), following English order. Confirm.
rulings.notes: The order of two or more adjectives (A4.22) is still undecided. See author_inputs_needed.

rulings.ruling: li may not be dropped after a side noun (nazru, zavme, silda, cemnu, lizma, rizno) used as a preposition.
examples: Li lavra semnesia nazru li nimu.
The bird sits behind the home.
examples_ungrammatical: li dropped after a side noun

rulings.ruling: maivo is deliberately both the pronoun 'I' and the noun 'Self'. Context decides.
examples: I am beautiful. / The Self is beautiful.
rulings.translator_preference: Always write the noun as li maivo, so translator output is never ambiguous.

rulings.topic: Which words take -ri, and plural agreement
rulings.ruling: -ri attaches to nouns, pronouns, demonstratives, and an adjective used as a noun after a determiner; never to a bare adjective or a verb. After any count word (a number, a quantifier, eliri or olari), -ri on the noun is optional, chosen by sound and meter. A singular demonstrative (eli, ola) takes a singular noun.
examples_ungrammatical: singular demonstrative with a plural noun
derived: 'A singular demonstrative takes a singular noun' makes the ✗ example of option B explicit. Confirm.

rulings.ruling: An animal is referred to with ito by default. A named animal takes saivo.
examples: Li lavra lirala; ito ka vanisan.
The bird sings; it is beautiful.
Nilo (the bird) sings; she is beautiful.
rulings.notes: sela (reflexive only, or also emphatic) and whether maivori includes the listener were not decided. See author_inputs_needed.

rulings.ruling: Only listed time adverbials stand bare as 'when': entries in the time-adverbial table, -krono correlatives, and day compounds (deyapressa, deyaapo, deyafutu). A plain time noun (merno, nullo, vesno, mambi, lornu …) used as 'when' takes en. A bare plain noun after a verb is its object.
rulings.notes: Duration ('for two days', 2.1:G55 bare measure after the object) still collides with an object reading. See author_inputs_needed.

rulings.topic: yuta, en, ko and la: one test per word
rulings.ruling: One test per word. yuta = a tool, means or substance handled or used up. en = a medium or state one is in, including a manner seen as a medium. ko = a companion, or an emotion that accompanies the act. la + adjective = the quality of the action.
examples: Maivo lallela li dorbi yuta li kemye.
I open the door with the key.
Saivo po senosia en baba melosan valla.
She spoke in a musical voice.
rulings.notes: The en/intra and transa/taro- overlaps named in I-25 were not decided.

rulings.ruling: la + adjective stands only among the adjuncts, after the verb and object. A degree word goes between la and the adjective: la ruli molusan.
Amounts: kasi or menu + noun … tamo NP. Manner: la kasi (or la menu) + adjective … tamo NP.
examples: Maivo tovota kasi lirari tamo taivo.
I have more songs than you.
Maivo lirala la kasi molusan tamo taivo.
I sing more gently than you.
examples_ungrammatical: bare kasi after the verb is not licensed (option B was not chosen)
rulings.notes: Comparing an action with no manner adjective ('I sing more than you', 'I love you more than …') still has no form. See author_inputs_needed.

rulings.ruling: gase + a number may mean 'about' or 'like'; context decides.
examples: I have about two coins. / … something like two coins.
rulings.translator_preference: For 'about N' write gase N; for a simile write gase li N (with the article), so output is unambiguous.

rulings.ruling: A measure (for kroti 'ago' and krotiapo 'from now') is NUMBER + unit, or a listed quantifier + unit. Listed quantifiers: AUTHOR INPUT NEEDED.
examples: Maivo po venreva kroti dossa deya.
rulings.notes: Do not invent the list. Until the author supplies it, treat only NUMBER + unit as a measure and report kroti + quantifier + noun as unresolved.

rulings.ruling: Valency operators vaku (make), lesvu (let) and tekvu (prevent): CAUSER [TENSE] [noma] [ne] [MODAL] … [EVIDENTIAL] OP ACTOR [ne] [APPROACH] [PHASE] [EFFORT] VERB [OBJECT]. Tense, modal and evidential belong to the main clause; the actor's own negation, approach, phase and effort follow the actor. The embedded verb may take an object.
examples: Maivo vaku saivo sapusia li nami.
I make him eat the food.

rulings.ruling: gome may passivise any verb that is attested with an object anywhere in the data. Without gome, the subject is the doer, except for the listed change-of-state verbs, whose subject may be the thing that changes (an anticausative reading).
examples: Li lira gome sarbisia gagu maivo.
The song is written by me.
Zafra, li dorbi po gome lallela.

rulings.topic: Adjective + sidu + verb: no dummy ito
rulings.ruling: In ADJECTIVE + sidu + VERB, the thing the adjective describes is the subject of the clause and the understood object of the verb. There is no dummy ito.
examples: Trana ke ruli levasan sidu zeldoza.
Change is very easy to resist.
examples_ungrammatical: Ito ke ruli levasan sidu zeldoza trana.
dummy ito with an overt object

rulings.ruling: A pronoun recipient may stand bare right after any verb whose meaning has a recipient (giving, lending, sending, owing, paying, bringing, teaching, showing, telling, singing to …). Otherwise, and always for a non-pronoun recipient, the recipient takes ala after the theme.
examples: Maivo lirala baba lira ala taivo.
I sing a song to you.

rulings.ruling: Purpose always uses kopisa. With the same subject, kopisa + bare verb phrase (no subject); with a different subject, kopisa + clause. sidu stays for verb chains (desida sidu lirala).
examples: Maivo po venreva eli-pago kopisa lirala.
I sing so that you dance.
examples_ungrammatical: Maivo po venreva eli-pago sidu lirala.
sidu is not used for purpose
rulings.notes: ke sidu ('destined to', open_questions_do_not_resolve[3]) stays open.

rulings.ruling: 'Would have' is always po noma viki. po viki without noma is not a form.
examples: Si maivo po noma masuma, taivo po noma viki relsira.
If I had asked, you would have answered.

rulings.topic: The comma that closes a raho clause
rulings.ruling: A raho clause that does not end the sentence is closed by a comma (a pause in speech) when it contains its own object or adjunct. A raho clause of only a verb (and its operators) needs no comma.
examples: Li nela raho lirala ka benasan.
The person who sings is good.
Li sabeyo raho vismava eli, ne yehu vimova li vordu.
The sage who studies this did not witness the word.
examples_ungrammatical: Li sabeyo raho vismava eli ne yehu vimova li vordu.
relative clause with an object, not closed by a comma

rulings.ruling: Hopeful purpose ('so that perhaps', 'in the hope that') is kopisa + a clause whose verb carries nosi. fime always introduces a content clause ('that').
examples: Maivo lirala, kopisa taivo nosi rilura.
I sing, so that perhaps you'll dance.
Maivo sabesia fime taivo nosi lirala.
I know that you might sing.

rulings.ruling: Clause-initial tonsi means 'therefore' and is followed by a comma. tonsi meaning 'so' (degree) stands only before a predicate adjective, after a copula.
examples: Taivo ke tonsi corvisan fime taivo viki savalisia maivo ki?
Are you so brave that you would kiss me?

rulings.ruling: An unmarked subordinate clause takes the main clause's tense, whatever its linker. sige clauses are the exception and always mark their own tense. A subordinate clause with its own tense word keeps it.
examples: Kureli taivo venreva, maivo po lirala.
As soon as you came, I sang.
Maivo po masuma ki-oro taivo relnura.
settles_open_questions: open_questions_do_not_resolve[5] (tense after kureli, sina, si, nevi)
rulings.notes: Clauses opened by clause adverbs (tonsi, narli, korsi, krotiata) and coordinated ata / nara clauses are main clauses, not subordinate, and are outside this rule.

rulings.ruling: A topic that is the subject of its clause must be picked up by a pronoun. A non-subject topic may be picked up or left as a gap; a gap is read as the verb's object.
examples: Li bumre hozi, Kipo po bumreba.
As for the bread, Kipo baked it.
Li bumre hozi, Kipo po bumreba ito.
As for the bread, Kipo baked it.
derived: 'A gap is read as the verb's object' resolves the remaining ambiguity of option C. Confirm.

rulings.topic: Relatives on a possessor, a time or a place
rulings.ruling: Relative clauses on a possessor, a time or a place use a resumptive pronoun in place, as 2.1:G52 does for prepositions: possessor → PRONOUN de NOUN; time or place → the needed preposition + ito.
examples: li lirayo raho maivo amora saivo de lira
the singer whose song I love
li krono raho maivo po lirala en ito
li pago raho maivo po venreva da ito

rulings.ruling: The motion prefixes are productive on any verb, with compositional meanings: va- = toward the speaker, here; du- = away, giving away; taro- = across, through; yave- = together, to meet; revo- = back, again. A listed meaning (the four curated phrases and any listed prefixed verb) overrides the compositional one. 'Motion verb' is no longer a category the grammar needs. lu-, nu-, mi-, so- stay retired.
rulings.notes: This also resolves I-06 (the undefined class of motion verbs).

rulings.ruling: -ti is an inflection-like suffix, not one of the derivations. Word ::= ROOT + (one form OR one derivation) + -ti + -ri; -ti may follow any form or derivation.
A word ending in pago is the same word whether read as ROOT + -pago or as a compound with the root pago. It is a noun with no further forms unless its dictionary line lists them.

rulings.topic: Image compounds have all seven forms
rulings.ruling: Image compounds have all seven forms, built by the ordinary form rules, with predictable meanings. This is an explicit exception to hard_rules[1] ('only listed forms exist'), which still governs every other headword.
derived: Proposed meaning templates, for confirmation: noun = the image; -asa = the image at its highest or sacred degree; -na = the absence or opposite of the image; verb = to make, do or bring about the image; -san = having the quality of the image; -asasan = supremely so; -nasan = lacking the image.
rulings.translator_preference: Prefer attested image compounds and their attested readings; use a predicted form only when no listed word fits, and flag it in the output.

rulings.ruling: Negative numbers: antizi + NUMBER (antizi dossa = minus two). antizi is a new function word.
rulings.notes: Decimals were not decided and remain outside the language.

function_words.position: number sign: directly before a number
